title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Psychiatric Comorbidity in a Patient with Charles Bonnet Syndrome
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman was referred to neurology for evaluation of complex symptoms. Her history began in her 20s with a motorcycle collision (no diagnosed TBI), followed by lifelong migraine headaches and syncope with transient vision loss on standing, confirmed by positive tilt-table testing. In 2007, she developed nocturnal whole-body shaking without loss of consciousness, diagnosed as nonepileptic seizures, refractory to levetiracetam. She also experienced intermittent right-sided shaking events associated with prolonged postictal sleep. Over subsequent years, she complained of progressive memory and comprehension difficulties, notably in doing laundry and operating familiar appliances. She denied mood symptoms. Examination revealed a positive Romberg sign and impaired tandem gait but preserved heel-to-toe walking. Video-EEG captured multiple nonepileptic spells without ictal discharges. By 2011–12, she reported worsening headaches and depth-perception problems; MRI showed frontal lobe atrophy. 

In May 2013, she began experiencing nightly complex visual hallucinations of people conversing with each other (never addressing her) accompanied by nonthreatening auditory hallucinations only during visual episodes. She retained insight—“I know these people aren’t really there, and they disappear when I turn on the lights.” She also saw “blue spots” over her left eye and hands and “cracks” on white walls. Fundoscopy revealed floaters. Her husband noted increasing forgetfulness. Neurologic examination found no cogwheel rigidity, no bradykinesia, no shuffling gait, and no gait instability. Cognitive testing yielded a MoCA score of 20/30. Routine labs including B12 and folate were unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. New-onset epilepsy — “The patient's history of documented NES most likely ruled out the development of new-onset epilepsy at the age of 70, although partial complex seizures could possibly account for her history of falls. However, the patient and her family's description of her NES made partial complex seizures less likely.”  
2. Dissociative phenomena (depersonalization) — “In line with the conceptualization of NES, there is a possibility that the patient's episodes of confusion and wandering alongside the feeling of unfamiliarity of her house might represent dissociative phenomena, specifically depersonalization … although the patient was not able to clearly identify any known stressors.”  
3. Pseudodementia / Alzheimer’s dementia — “When the patient had MOCA scores completed, pseudodementia was initially considered given severity of documented depression and anxiety. However, the patient's ability to perform the majority of her ADLs and IADLs as well as having no clinically apparent anomia, aphasia, or apraxia made mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's less likely.”  
4. Lewy-Body dementia — “Once the patient was found to have memory and cognitive impairment alongside fall frequency, the diagnosis of Lewy-Body Dementia was then considered. However, of the clinical symptomatic triad of fluctuating cognitive impairment, extrapyramidal features, and visual hallucinations, the patient primarily had only the latter once her clonazepam was tapered and discontinued, making LBD less likely. Furthermore, the patient did not demonstrate any extrapyramidal symptoms or clinical sensitivity to quetiapine, an atypical antipsychotic, which definitively goes against the diagnosis of LBD.”  
5. Parkinson’s dementia — “Her history of myriad falls was initially thought to be due to a combination of either NES or syncope … and thus their attribution to Parkinsonism was thought less likely.”  
6. Formal thought disorder / schizophrenia — “Much less likely was that the patient presented with first onset formal thought disorder at the age of 70.”  
7. Migraine aura / headache-related phenomena — “The patient's once or twice monthly to near daily chronic headaches or transformed migraines were associated with ‘flashing lights,’ and so the notion that her vision was compromised at baseline (‘problems with depth perception’) was not on the forefront of our conceptualization towards the possibility of Charles Bonnet Syndrome until much later in her clinical course.”  
8. Charles Bonnet syndrome — considered given complex visual hallucinations in the setting of ocular pathology, preserved insight, and disappearance of images in bright light.
